questions.question: Name the eight design considerations that decide fitness for purpose and define any four of them.
questions.expected_answer: Users, purpose, function, cost-effectiveness, safety, ergonomics, aesthetics, and impact on society and the environment. Users: who will use the product and what they are like. Purpose: the need the product exists to meet. Function: what the product does and how well, judged against the purpose. Cost-effectiveness: value gained for what the product costs to make, buy and run, not mere cheapness. Safety: whether the product can harm the user or others. Ergonomics: how well the product fits the human body and the effort needed to use it. Aesthetics: how it looks and feels. Impact: its effects on communities, jobs and fairness, and on the natural world over its whole life.

questions.question: Use the paraffin stove to explain why a product that works can still be unfit for purpose.
questions.expected_answer: The paraffin stove has good function and is cost-effective: it cooks food cheaply where there is no electricity, which is why millions of homes use it. But it fails on safety, with an open flame, a tank of flammable fuel and a light frame that tips, causing burns and shack fires; it has poor ergonomics if controls are low; and it has harmful impacts on society, filling hospital wards, and on the environment, burning fossil fuel and releasing smoke indoors. Because fitness for purpose is judged on all considerations together, a working product that injures its users and harms others is not fit for purpose.

questions.question: Apply at least five of the considerations to the model rescue device and show how each one adds to the design brief.
questions.expected_answer: Users: Grade 7 learners and the teacher, so the hand syringe must suit a child's grip. Purpose and function: to demonstrate hydraulics and levers producing a controlled force, so the jaws must open and grip visibly. Cost-effectiveness: free provided materials and a small budget for extras. Safety: no sharp edges, water instead of oil, syringes never pointed at anyone. Ergonomics: a flat stable base and an easy one-handed push. Aesthetics: neat, labelled, perhaps in rescue colours. Impact: cardboard recycled and syringes reused afterwards, with a note on how the real tool serves society.
